segment_name: Opening: The Closed Door of Heriot Row

questions.question: Caroline, you said something in our pre-chat that I keep coming back to — you called that famous morning passage 'the bait.' Can you read it for us and explain what you mean by that? Because on the surface it's gorgeous — it feels like Oliphant is handing us a heroine.
questions.intent: Get Caroline to read c5:p27 aloud and deliver her 'trap' thesis early, setting up immediate disagreement from James about whether it's irony or institutional critique — and from Eleanor about whether the trap is in the *syntax* rather than the tone

questions.question: Eleanor, I know you want to push back on the 'romantic optimism' reading — and you made this point about the *sentence construction* itself being ironic. What does that actually mean for a reader? Like, can you show us in the text where the conditional framing does that work?
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to do close textual analysis of c5:p27, specifically the 'what in human form could have given' construction — and provoke Caroline to agree on irony while disagreeing on where it lives (tone vs. syntax)

questions.question: James, I want to put something to you directly — both Eleanor and Caroline are talking about irony and syntax and traps, and it's all very literary. But your argument is more brutal than that, isn't it? It's not that the *sentence* is ironic — it's that the *world* doesn't care about Hester's latent possibilities. Is that a different claim?
questions.intent: Force James to articulate the institutional critique as distinct from the literary-irony reading, and see if Eleanor or Caroline feel the need to defend the primacy of craft over context

questions.question: Okay, so we've been circling Catherine's cry in c41 — 'Is there no reason in it when God's creature lifts a face of anguish to His throne?' Can you read that passage for us, Caroline? Because you said this is where the novel's conscience actually lives — not in Hester at all. That's a pretty bold claim about whose novel this is.
questions.intent: Get Caroline to read c41:p3 aloud and make the case that Catherine is the novel's moral center — directly provoking James to agree for different reasons and Eleanor to redirect toward the formal properties of the apostrophe and repetition

questions.question: Eleanor, I have to ask — because you used the word 'liturgical' about that passage, which is striking. You're saying Oliphant turns Catherine's grief into something almost like prayer. But does that make it more powerful or does it risk turning real suffering into *performance*? Is there a cost to that kind of formal control?
questions.intent: Push Eleanor on whether Oliphant's formal artistry aestheticizes Catherine's pain in a way that undercuts James's institutional reading or Caroline's theological one — create a three-way tension about what the 'literary' does to the 'real'

steering_notes: Open with the bait-and-trap thesis because it's the most accessible hook — everyone agrees on it but for different reasons, and that productive agreement-with-disagreement is good early energy. Keep pushing the distinction between 'the irony is in the prose' (Eleanor), 'the irony is in the characterisation' (Caroline), and 'irony doesn't even matter — the institutions are the point' (James). The Catherine question is the pivot for the second half of the segment; make sure it doesn't get lost as a footnote to the Hester discussion. If time is short, cut Q3 and fold James's institutional argument into Q2 as a challenge.
cross_engagement_targets: Eleanor and Caroline both read c5:p27 as ironic but locate that irony differently — Eleanor in the conditional syntax, Caroline in the characterisation gap. Ask them directly whether those are the same claim or competing ones.

James's argument that 'nature and optimism mean nothing against bankruptcy law' is a direct challenge to Eleanor's 'structural realism' framing — Eleanor might actually agree with him more than she thinks, but call it craft where he calls it ideology. Surface that.

Caroline says Catherine's cry 'breaks theodicy' and Oliphant never answers it. James says it's a specific indictment of Victorian institutions. Eleanor says the *form* of the utterance is the point. These are three genuinely different readings of the same passage — make them talk to each other rather than past each other.

segment_name: A Woman of Business: Catherine's Paradox

questions.question: Eleanor, you've got this phrase 'casuistry of love' — c35:p100 — and you've called it the key to Catherine's entire character. But I want to push on the word 'casuistry' itself. Is Oliphant admiring Catherine's intelligence here, or condemning it? Because those feel like very different novels.
questions.intent: Open the central interpretive fault line on Catherine — get Eleanor to commit to the 'tragedy of consciousness' reading before Blackstone and Woodcourt can complicate it

questions.question: James, you'd say that's too generous — that Catherine isn't *failing* to see reality, the system is actively protecting her from having to. So is the 'casuistry' not really Catherine's achievement at all? Is it just... what money buys you?
questions.intent: Force the structural vs psychological disagreement into the open — get Blackstone to argue the institutions do the self-deception *for* Catherine, which directly challenges Eleanor's 'brilliant woman' reading

questions.question: Caroline, you want to read that passage in c13:p29 — Catherine finding the Hester-and-Harry idea 'strangely funny' but also taking 'a strange blow.' Because I think that moment might be the tell. Is Catherine laughing because she doesn't understand Hester, or because she understands her perfectly well and can't afford to admit it?
questions.intent: Draw out Woodcourt's take on Catherine's self-knowledge versus self-deception — and set up the disagreement with Hartley about whether Catherine's business persona was ever 'real'

questions.question: Caroline, I need you to read the passage at c42:p0 — the 'guilty pair in Paradise' sentence — because you've said the biblical weight transforms the whole thing. But Blackstone, I know you'd resist the idea that this gives Hester and Edward equal moral standing. So after Caroline reads it, I want to hear from both of you.
questions.intent: Get the passage read aloud for radio impact, then trigger the direct Woodcourt-Blackstone disagreement about whether the Eden language implies shared culpability or just elevates Hester's suffering

questions.question: James, Hester's accusation to Edward in c15:p40 — 'you have proved that it was true, and I a fool' — you've called that devastating. But Eleanor makes a good point: Oliphant never actually shows us Edward answering it. What does that silence *do*? Is Oliphant letting Edward off the hook, or is she saying the system never required him to answer in the first place?
questions.intent: Force the question of Edward's narrative absence and whether it's moral or structural — brings all three experts into direct collision over whether the novel is a psychological portrait or a systemic critique

steering_notes: The core tension in this segment is psychological versus structural: Eleanor and Caroline both want to read Catherine as a complex interior portrait, while Blackstone wants to show the institutions doing the work Catherine gets credit (or blame) for. Don't let Blackstone's structural argument become a lecture — keep pulling it back to specific moments in the text. The 'casuistry of love' passage is the centrepiece and all three experts want to quote it, so let that happen once, richly, rather than three times. Use the c42:p0 reading as an energy reset if the conversation gets too abstract — hearing it aloud will reground everyone. Watch for the moment when Eleanor and Blackstone almost agree (Edward's silence) and push into it rather than past it.
cross_engagement_targets: Eleanor reads Catherine as a 'tragedy of consciousness' — her intelligence becomes the instrument of her own destruction. Blackstone thinks this misses the point entirely: Catherine's not tragic, she's *protected*. That's the sharpest disagreement in the segment and should be surfaced early.

Caroline argues Oliphant's moral generosity toward Catherine — she gets to go home happy — is actually more radical than punishment would be. Eleanor thinks Catherine has *nothing* when her self-narration collapses. These are almost opposite readings of the ending and neither has noticed the other holds the inverse position.
All three experts want to quote c35:p100 — use that convergence to ask what they *disagree* about in the same sentence, rather than letting three people say the same thing in succession.

segment_name: The Weight of Propriety: Social Chains and Female Constraint

questions.question: Eleanor, you've made this really striking claim that the novel doesn't just *describe* female constraint—it actually *performs* it in the grammar and sentence structure. Like, Catherine's power always arrives in the past tense, reported, at a distance. Can you walk us through what you mean by that? Because I think that's either a brilliant reading or a completely maddening one, and I want to hear you make the case.
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to articulate her formal/structural argument about narrative-as-constraint before Blackstone can challenge it on ideological grounds—sets up the core tension of the segment

questions.question: James, I have to put this to you directly: you've called Mrs. John Vernon in that opening scene—the scarf, the white shoulders, the Lawrence portrait comparison—you've called it 'portraiture as imprisonment.' But Caroline thinks Oliphant is actually *sympathizing* with the woman trapped in that pose. Who's right? Because you're both looking at exactly the same passage.
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Blackstone's structural-critique reading and Woodcourt's sympathetic reading of c1:p90—get them to disagree on what tone Oliphant actually strikes

questions.question: Caroline, you want to read Hester as the one honest person in a world of performance—she's the one who says 'I am a woman but I am not a fool, try me.' But James would say that speech isn't rebellion, it's *pleading*. She has no legal standing, no access to information, no way to act. Does demanding to be included in the truth actually *do* anything in this novel, or is it just a more sophisticated form of helplessness?
questions.intent: Draw out Woodcourt's strongest defence of Hester's agency while letting Blackstone's structural pessimism pressure it—creates a genuine three-way tension about what 'resistance' means when you have no institutional power

questions.question: Eleanor, read us the death scene—the ivory head, the chill creeping in. Because you've described it as 'architecturally perfect,' and Caroline finds it almost unbearably moving, and I want to know whether those are the same response or completely different ones. Is Oliphant making us feel grief here, or is she making an argument?
questions.intent: Get the passage at c45:p30 read aloud—then force a distinction between aesthetic response and structural argument, which maps onto the Hartley/Woodcourt divide and will provoke Blackstone to say something provocative about sentimentalism

questions.question: James, Captain Morgan asks—and you've flagged this—'Is it just that one human creature should be made the victim of another, simply because he has been instrumental in bringing that other into the world?' And you've pointed out that nobody actually *answers* him in the novel. Do you think Oliphant *has* an answer? Or is she deliberately leaving that question burning?
questions.intent: Draw out Blackstone's take on the novel's political ambition versus its refusal to resolve—sets up a potential disagreement with Woodcourt who wants to sit with the discomfort, and with Hartley who reads it as structural inevitability rather than authorial evasion

steering_notes: The segment has a natural arc: start with form and technique (Eleanor), move into character and sympathy (the Mrs. Vernon confrontation between James and Caroline), then land on Hester's demand for inclusion, then the death scene as the emotional peak, then end on the Captain's unanswered question which leaves the room with something unresolved. Don't let Blackstone dominate early—his structural argument is strongest as a *response* to what Eleanor and Caroline set up. The real radio gold is the moment when Caroline and James realise they're both sympathetic to Oliphant but for completely opposite reasons: she's either exposing the cruelty of the system or compassionating those trapped in it. Push them on whether those readings are actually compatible. Watch out for the segment becoming too academic—keep pulling back to the physical, sensory language: the scarf, the white shoulders, the ivory, the chill. That's where the emotion lives.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone calls Mrs. Vernon's Lawrence-portrait pose 'pathetic'; Woodcourt calls it sympathetic—this is a direct contradiction on the same passage (c1:p90) and should be surfaced as early as possible

Blackstone reads Hester's 'I am a woman but I am not a fool' speech as pleading for inclusion rather than genuine rebellion; Woodcourt hears it as 'epistemological equality' that 'sings when read aloud'—get them to disagree on the *register* of that speech

Hartley argues Catherine's power is constructed through passive voice and reported speech, never her own interiority—Blackstone agrees she's not a genuine institutional agent, but for different reasons (health, unwed status, male forbearance). They're arriving at the same conclusion by opposite routes; surface that

All three experts want to quote c45:p30 (the death scene)—make this a moment of convergence before letting them diverge on what it *means*: grief (Woodcourt), structural inevitability (Hartley), or the temperature of a life that never broke its rules (also Woodcourt, beautifully)

segment_name: Hester's Unquiet Heart: Ambition and Betrayal

questions.question: Eleanor, you said before we started that reading Oliphant aloud is almost the point — that the rhythm *is* the meaning. There's this sentence at c9:p12 that you're dying to get to: 'She understood no reason for it, but she understood it.' Can you just read that and tell us why those eight words stopped you in your tracks?
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to read the passage aloud and articulate her case for Oliphant as a prose stylist, opening the door for Caroline to agree from an emotional angle and James to reframe it politically

questions.question: Caroline, there's a moment at c9:p28 where an old clerk describes Hester's mother handing over her life savings — twenty pounds — and he does it 'with a little laugh.' You called that laugh heartbreaking. James might call it an indictment. Who's right?
questions.intent: Use the disagreement between Caroline's emotional reading and James's structural one to generate genuine debate over whether the twenty pounds scene is about maternal dignity or systemic exclusion

questions.question: James, you want people to be angry at c9:p20 — Catherine sitting there confident, 'not afraid of evil tidings,' everyone silent around her. You read that silence as institutional, not personal. But isn't that a bit cold? Isn't Oliphant also just showing us a woman we're about to watch be destroyed?
questions.intent: Challenge James to defend his structural reading against the more empathetic character reading Caroline favors, and see if Eleanor can find a third position about how the silence is *constructed* by the narration

questions.question: All three of you have flagged c9:p32 — Hester asking 'Where was my father?' Eleanor says she's seizing narrative control, James says she's asking a legal question the novel has been avoiding, you say it's visceral before it's intellectual. So which is it — is Hester doing something brave, something angry, or something cold?
questions.intent: Force direct comparison of all three expert readings of the same line; get them to disagree about whether Hester's agency here is emotional, intellectual, or political

questions.question: James, you said Hester's 'unquiet heart' isn't ambition — it's rational fury. But Eleanor would say it's hermeneutical awakening, and Caroline would say it's bodily, it's nerves. Is there actually a difference, or are all three of you just describing the same thing in different dialects?
questions.intent: Force a direct meta-disagreement about how to read Hester's interiority and whether their three frameworks are genuinely incompatible or secretly complementary — good closing energy

steering_notes: This segment has a natural arc: move from the prose texture (Eleanor's sentence, c9:p12) through the emotional gut-punch of the twenty pounds (c9:p28) to the political explosion of 'Where was my father?' (c9:p32). Let the first question be generous and almost lyrical — get the sound of Oliphant in the room early. The heat builds. James and Caroline are going to clash on whether Catherine's blindness is a character flaw or a structural indictment; let that run. The real prize is the final question: all three experts have staked claims on the same line at c9:p32 and their readings are genuinely different. Don't let anyone monopolize it. If energy flags, just ask someone to read the passage aloud — Eleanor especially will run with that.
cross_engagement_targets: Eleanor frames Catherine's obliviousness as a narratorial construction; Caroline and James both treat it more as a character or social condition — push Eleanor to explain what the difference actually means in practice
James reads the twenty pounds as evidence of institutional powerlessness; Caroline reads it as dignity — these are not compatible and neither wants to give ground. Let them go.
All three converge on c9:p32 with different frameworks (legal/structural vs hermeneutical vs visceral) — this is the segment's richest cross-engagement moment and should not be resolved too quickly

Caroline accuses both Eleanor and James of missing the 'bodily' dimension of Hester's awakening; Eleanor will likely agree the word 'thrill' is doing physical work but reframe it — worth drawing out explicitly

segment_name: The Machinery of Ruin: Edward's Speculation and the Logic of Flight

questions.question: Caroline, you said in our chat beforehand that you want to read the addiction passage aloud — the brandy and laudanum line — and I think we should just start there. Can you read it for us and tell us why that sentence stopped you in your tracks?
questions.intent: Open the segment with a live reading that immediately establishes the psychological register; let the prose do the work before any analysis begins

questions.question: James, you've pushed back quite hard on the idea that this is really about Edward's psychology at all — you think it's institutional, structural, a legal trap. But Caroline and Eleanor are both drawn to the interiority of it, the *compulsion*. Are they just romanticising what is actually a very cold, rational calculation?
questions.intent: Force the structural vs psychological disagreement into the open; get Blackstone to defend his 'rational actor' reading against the addiction framing

questions.question: Eleanor, I want to bring you in on something specific — you said the artillery image is doing three jobs at once, simile, foreshadowing, psychological portrait, all in one sentence. Can you read it and actually walk us through that? Because I think that's either going to convince James entirely or annoy him enormously.
questions.intent: Get a close reading of the artillery passage that tests whether the psychological and structural readings are actually compatible or genuinely in conflict

questions.question: James, Eleanor's reading there treats the language as the *meaning* — the metaphors are the diagnosis. But you keep wanting to pull us back to real legal structures, real financial instruments. Is Oliphant actually that careful about the economic specifics, or is she using financial speculation as a kind of shorthand for something more personal?
questions.intent: Probe whether Blackstone thinks Oliphant earns the structural reading or whether the novel is ultimately more interested in character than institution; push him toward either conceding ground or doubling down

questions.question: I want to end on something a bit uncomfortable. Eleanor, you said earlier that Oliphant forces us to experience Edward's fantasy as *thrilling* — and Caroline, you've described this as the story of a man who could have been good. But doesn't that sympathy have a cost? Catherine hasn't done anything wrong. She's 'unconscious', as Oliphant puts it. Are we in danger of being seduced by the same fantasy Edward is?
questions.intent: Land on the novel's ethical provocation — does the reader's sympathy for Edward implicate us? Set up a three-way disagreement about where Oliphant's moral compass is actually pointing

steering_notes: This segment has a strong risk of becoming too academic — three smart people who all agree Edward is sympathetic and the prose is remarkable. Push hard on the structural vs psychological fault line between Blackstone and the other two. The live readings are essential: make sure Caroline gets the addiction line, Eleanor gets the artillery passage, and Blackstone gets his 'ruin them all' quote. Don't let the conversation settle into appreciation — keep asking who is actually *right* about what Oliphant is doing and why it matters.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone's 'rational actor' framing directly contradicts Hartley and Woodcourt's compulsion/addiction reading — this is the central tension to keep returning to

Hartley's claim that the papers are the real protagonist sits interestingly against Blackstone's claim that the papers are real financial instruments, not symbols — they're making the same point from opposite directions without knowing it
Woodcourt's warmer, sadder Oliphant vs Blackstone's structuralist Oliphant — is the irony in these passages cold and diagnostic or genuinely mournful? Get them to argue about tone
All three want to defend Edward to some degree — use the Catherine question to destabilise that consensus and see who blinks first

segment_name: Irony and Intimacy: How Oliphant Reveals What Cannot Be Said

questions.question: Caroline, you said something in our chat that really stuck with me — that the irony in this novel isn't imposed from above, it's *inside* the moment. Can you take us into that passage in chapter 21 where Hester's heart is beating faster and she knows 'there was something more'? What's Oliphant actually doing there that a less skilled writer would get completely wrong?
questions.intent: Open the segment with the most seductive, intimate reading of the central technique — establish the body-as-truth-teller argument — and set up Blackstone's structural counter

questions.question: James, I can hear you itching to complicate that. Because you've argued that this gap between what's said and what's felt isn't just emotionally interesting — it's evidence of something much more coercive. That when Hester and Catherine speak in banter and indirection, it's not a stylistic choice, it's because direct speech was genuinely dangerous. Can you make that case?
questions.intent: Provoke the structural-coercion argument against the intimacy readings — get him to argue the irony is institutional violence, not narrative tenderness

questions.question: Eleanor, I want to give you a chance to fight back there, because you have a very different account of what the narrator is doing. You used the phrase 'imaginative generosity' — the idea that knowing more than the characters is actually an act of love, not superiority. Does Blackstone's reading kill that for you, or can both things be true at once?
questions.intent: Draw out the irony-as-intimacy argument and force a direct collision with Blackstone's coercion thesis — also get her to quote c5:p34 on the nested syntax if possible

questions.question: Let's go to Catherine Vernon, because I think this is where you three might actually disagree most sharply. There's that moment in chapter 8 — 'I did not stoop down to paltry work. I took a place which — others had abandoned' — and Caroline, you said you could *hear* the performance cracking. What's cracking exactly? Is Catherine lying to herself, or is she doing something more complicated?
questions.intent: Get the Catherine reading on the table — provoke disagreement between Woodcourt's ambiguity, Hartley's generosity reading, and Blackstone's shame-as-survival argument — target c8:p21 for quotation

questions.question: Eleanor, you've talked about the branding image in chapter 7 — 'branded upon her as by red-hot irons' — as doing emotional work that language alone can't do. But James would say that branding is also literal: a woman marked by family scandal in Victorian England loses real options, legal and economic ones. And Caroline thinks it's actually liberating. So what is the branding *doing* — is it wound, or freedom, or both?
questions.intent: Force all three readings of c7:p89 into direct collision — wound vs liberation vs institutional marking — this should be the segment's most contested moment

steering_notes: Let Caroline open with the intimate, sensation-based reading so the segment starts warm and literary before Blackstone introduces structural friction. The key tension is between Hartley and Woodcourt's shared investment in interiority and Blackstone's insistence that the silence is coerced not chosen — push that fault line hard in the middle questions. Don't let Blackstone dominate with context; keep pulling back to the actual sentences. The branding passage is the best collision point — save it for last when the disagreement is already live. If energy dips, ask someone to just read a passage aloud before explaining it.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone's claim that indirection is 'institutional violence' directly contradicts Hartley's claim that the narrator's omniscience is 'imaginative generosity' — these are incompatible framings of the same technique and need to be named as such on air

Woodcourt reads the branding in c7:p89 as liberating agency; Blackstone reads it as legal and economic marking; Hartley reads it as emotional devastation that accelerates maturity — three readings of one image, force them to negotiate

Hartley insists the unsayable is *known* through the narrator's access to sensation, not suppressed; Blackstone insists it's suppressed by law and custom — this is the deepest disagreement and should surface around the c21:p99 passage

Woodcourt and Hartley both want to protect Catherine's complexity from reductive readings, but Hartley leans toward generosity while Woodcourt leans toward ambiguity — a productive internal difference that Blackstone's shame-as-survival reading might unexpectedly support

questions.question: Caroline, you said something in our conversation that really stuck with me—that Hester doesn't just want to restore her mother, she wants to *erase* Catherine's legitimacy. And that the moment she imagines that, she's already lost something. Can you take us to that portrait passage and explain why you think the act of hanging that picture back up would actually disqualify Hester from the very redemption she's chasing?
questions.intent: Get Caroline to read and unpack c12:p38 and articulate the corruption-through-restoration paradox, which sets up a direct challenge from Eleanor

questions.question: Eleanor, I know you want to push back on that—because you've been arguing that the portrait image is actually *architecture*, that it's about displacement and restoration in a formally sophisticated way. Is Oliphant really indicting Hester there, or is she doing something more ambiguous with the prose itself?
questions.intent: Draw out Eleanor's formalist reading of the portrait passage and her argument that the novel performs rather than resolves the moral question, creating direct friction with Caroline's more moralistic reading

questions.question: James, I want to bring you in here because I think you'd say both Eleanor and Caroline are missing the bigger picture—that it almost doesn't matter whether Hester is corrupted or redeemed, because the system she's operating in makes the distinction meaningless. She ends up managing the almshouse. Is that a happy ending, a sad one, or is Oliphant doing something much colder than either?
questions.intent: Get Blackstone to articulate his structural indictment reading and his claim that the ending exposes the limits of redemption as a concept for women in these institutions—and to push back on both Eleanor's formal reading and Caroline's tragic one

questions.question: Eleanor, I have to ask you about that vertigo passage—'there would seem nothing to stand on, nothing to look up to, the skies would all whirl and the solid ground'—because you said reading it aloud is the only way to really feel what Oliphant is doing. Would you do that for us? And then tell me: is that dizziness Hester's emotion, or is it something Oliphant is actually doing *to* us?
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to read the passage aloud for radio effect, then articulate her strongest take—that the prose form enacts the vertigo rather than describing it—which both James and Caroline have different frameworks for interpreting

questions.question: Last question, and I want all three of you to have a go at this: the novel is called *Hester*. Not *The Vernons* or *Catherine* or *The White House*. Oliphant put this woman's name on the cover, and then—James, you'd say—left her trapped. Caroline, you'd say left her exhausted. Eleanor, you'd say left her suspended. So what is Oliphant actually claiming about this character? Does Hester earn her title?
questions.intent: Force a direct three-way confrontation on the novel's ultimate stance toward Hester—redemption, indictment, or formal suspension—and give each expert a chance to land their strongest final take

steering_notes: This segment has real heat in it—all three experts are reading the same passages and arriving at genuinely different conclusions, which is exactly what you want. Let the portrait passage and the vertigo passage do the work; don't rush past them. Eleanor and Caroline have the most direct friction (sympathetic formalism vs. moral corruption reading), but James is the one who pulls the rug out from under both of them by questioning whether redemption is even a meaningful category here. Save his structural argument for after Eleanor and Caroline have committed to their positions, so he's actually responding to something. The almshouse ending is the crux—push everyone back to it. If the conversation gets too abstract, remind them that Hester is a young woman who ends up working in a charity house still answerable to the woman who displaced her family. What does Oliphant want us to feel about that?
cross_engagement_targets: Eleanor argues the portrait image is formal architecture; Caroline argues it's moral self-corruption—these are directly incompatible and should be staged as a direct exchange after question 1 and 2

James's claim that Hester's rejection of Harry is about recognizing structural futility rather than moral growth directly contradicts Eleanor's reading of it as performed redemption—flag this explicitly and ask Eleanor to respond

Caroline's reading of the vertigo as 'what you feel when you're about to do something wrong' versus James's reading of it as 'rational response to structural powerlessness' is the sharpest disagreement in the segment and should anchor the discussion of the vertigo passage in question 4

All three experts want to quote the same three passages—use this as a feature, not a bug: point out on air that they've all flagged the same lines and ask why those particular words keep pulling critics back
